intro.html: All ten of these verbs mean speaking against someone, but they differ in three ways: how hard (a gentle warning or a furious scolding), how official (a friend’s comment or a vote by a council) and how (scolding, mocking or belittling).

From gentlest to harshest, roughly: admonish (warn gently) → reproach (show disappointment) → rebuke and reprimand (scold sharply or formally) → chastise and berate (scold severely, angrily, at length). Censure and denounce are formal and public; deride and disparage belittle with scorn.

words.ex: The school board voted to {censure} the member who leaked the private report.
words.ctx: The league did not suspend the coach, but it did {censure} him in a public statement, calling his behavior toward the referee unacceptable.
words.etym: From Latin censura, the office of a Roman censor, an official who judged citizens’ conduct, from censere, “to assess.”
words.note: Censure (to blame formally) is not censor (to cut out parts of a book, film or letter).

mn.cue: SEN-SURE: the council is SURE you were wrong
mn.text: The whole council stands up and votes together: they are sure their member broke the rules. To {censure} is to blame someone officially.

scene.alt: Two council members point at a man who broke the rules, under a banner.

words.ex: The lifeguard {rebuked} the boys for running on the wet deck.
words.ctx: Instead of praising her for finishing early, the teacher {rebuked} her for rushing, pointing to three careless mistakes on the first page.

mn.text: When Kai knocks the books off the shelf a second time, the librarian snaps, “Not again, young man!” She {rebukes} him sharply.

scene.alt: A librarian sharply scolds a boy who has knocked books onto the floor again.

words.def: to tell someone you are disappointed in what they did
words.ex: Grandma did not yell; she simply {reproached} him with a sad shake of her head.
words.ctx: Lila {reproached} her brother for forgetting their mother’s birthday, not angrily but in a quiet voice that made him feel even worse.

mn.text: Mom approaches the broken lamp, sighs and says, “I expected better from you.” To {reproach} someone is to show your disappointment in them.

scene.alt: A disappointed mother looks at a knocked-over lamp while her son shrugs sheepishly beside a ball.

words.def: to warn or scold gently but firmly
words.ex: The coach {admonished} the players to drink water before practice.
words.ctx: The librarian did not shout at the giggling students; she simply {admonished} them, with a finger to her lips, to keep their voices down.
words.etym: From Latin admonere, “to remind, warn”: ad (to) + monere (to warn).
words.note: Admonish is the gentlest word in this topic.

mn.text: “Helmet on, please,” says Mom, in her gentle but firm Mom-ish way. To {admonish} is to warn someone gently but firmly.

scene.alt: A mother gently reminds her daughter to put on her helmet before riding her bike.

words.def: to scold formally, as a boss or official does
words.ex: The manager {reprimanded} the clerk for leaving the register open.
words.ctx: Because it was his third late arrival this month, the captain {reprimanded} the guard in writing, and a copy went into his file.
words.etym: From French réprimande, from Latin reprimenda, “things to be held back,” from reprimere, “to press back, check.”

mn.cue: a RAP on the HAND from the boss
mn.text: The boss calls Dev into her office and gives him a formal rap on the hand for the late report. To {reprimand} is to scold officially.

scene.alt: A boss in her office formally scolds a young worker holding a late report.

words.ex: The farmer {chastised} his son for leaving the barn door open all night.
words.ctx: The critic {chastised} the city for letting the old theater fall apart, calling the neglect a disgrace to everyone who had ever loved the place.

mn.text: The farmer chases the goats out of his garden, scolding them hard the whole way. To {chastise} is to scold or punish severely.

scene.alt: An angry farmer chases two goats out of his garden, scolding them.

words.def: to scold angrily and at length
words.ex: The fan {berated} the umpire for ten straight minutes over one call.
words.ctx: Rather than calmly explain the mistake, the chef {berated} the new cook in front of the whole kitchen, shouting about the burnt rice long after the pot was cleaned.

mn.text: Rex rants at the umpire for ten whole minutes over one call, shouting and stomping. To {berate} someone is to scold them angrily and at length.

scene.alt: A furious fan shouts on and on at a tired umpire.

words.def: to mock and make fun of with scorn
words.ex: Some kids {derided} her homemade costume, but it won first prize.
words.ctx: Experts once {derided} the idea of a phone without buttons as a silly toy; within a few years, nearly everyone carried one.
words.etym: From Latin deridere, “to laugh at, mock”: de (down) + ridere (to laugh), the root of ridiculous.

mn.text: The older kids point and laugh at Pip’s homemade cart: “Ha! You call that a ride?” To {deride} is to mock with scorn.

scene.alt: Two older boys point and laugh at a younger boy’s homemade wagon.

words.def: to speak of something as if it had little worth
words.ex: He {disparaged} his sister’s painting as “just a bunch of blobs.”
words.ctx: It is easy to {disparage} a small library as old-fashioned, but for many families in town it is the only place with free books and computers.
words.etym: From Old French desparagier, “to marry beneath one’s rank,” and so to lower or degrade.

mn.text: Victor stands at the curb and disses the whole parade: “Silly floats, tiny band, nothing special.” To {disparage} something is to talk about it as if it had little worth.

scene.alt: A sour man with crossed arms belittles a cheerful parade of teens with a drum and a flag.

words.def: to declare publicly that something is wrong or evil
words.ex: The mayor {denounced} the dumping of trash in the river.
words.ctx: Within hours, every club in the league had {denounced} the vandalism, calling it a shameful attack on a field that children used every day.
words.etym: From Latin denuntiare, “to announce officially, warn”: de + nuntiare (to announce).

mn.text: From the town hall steps, the mayor announces to everyone that dumping trash in the river is wrong and must stop. To {denounce} is to declare publicly that something is wrong.

scene.alt: A mayor with a megaphone publicly speaks out against dumping trash, beside a save our river sign.

after.cap: Three questions sort the ten words: how hard, how official, and how.

after.html: Censure and censor look alike. To censure is to blame formally (the senate censured him). To censor is to cut out material (the letter was censored).

choices: The council voted to censure the member who broke the rules.
The network will censure the bad words out of the movie.
The soldiers had to censure every letter home.
She asked the librarian to censure the dictionary.
items.why: Censure means to blame formally. Cutting words out of a movie or letter is censor, a different word.
To admonish is to warn gently but firmly. Berate and chastise are severe; denounce is a strong public condemnation.

items.q: The older students derided the freshman’s idea. They…
items.why: Deride means to mock with scorn; it comes from Latin ridere, “to laugh,” like ridiculous.

items.q: True or false: to berate someone is to scold them angrily and at length.
items.why: True. Berate is one of the harshest words here: a long, angry scolding.
